But when a commission of which the present Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) was a member, tells us-and I read the report to the committee-that the Grand Trunk Railway failed to maintain its roadbed and rolling stock in first class condition; when the three commissioners agree on that; when, as early as 1916, when their report was finally concluded, they said that the company were at that time $21,000,000 behind, which should have been put into the maintenance of the roadbed and rolling stock, but which was attributed to dividends, and when negotiations have been going on since then between the Government and the company for the purchase of the system, we know that the Grand Trunk officials would not be likely to advise their company to go into any further expenditure for maintenance of roadbed or rolling stock pending the negotiations. The verbal information that the Minister of Railways has given to the committee is not the kind of information to which the committee is entitled. And when the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) says to the committee: We are ready to give you the information; we invite you to ask for information; I say that it is simply fooling the people of Canada and' endeavouring, through the press gallery, to carry to the people the impression that all the information is contained in this little book which was printed yesterday and distributed to-day to the members. In this little book you will find, it is true, a copy of the correspondence and some statistics, but it gives no further information than can be found in the Blue Book on Railway Statistics published last year by the Department of. Railways. As to the exact expenditure that the country is now asked to assume and to which we commit the country, there is no information forthcoming, and we get to our queries evasive answers. That, I say, is not the proper way to treat the committee and the people of Canada. If we must carry this through now, if we must study it, we are entitled to more good faith-some further information and clearer 'answers than those which have been given this -afternoon.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Of course, if we stayed here for half a century, hon. gentlemen would have ingenuity enough to ask for something that would keep us here for another half century.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: You cannot complain up to now.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: We 'have been asked this afternoon as I recall the questions, for three things. The first is >a list of the 100,000 or 180,000 shareholders of the Grand Trunk; the second is to know what the American Government think of this proposition, and the third is to know how much money we think it will take to put the road into, as I presume the hon. member means, reasonable condition. I have already dealt with the first, and as the suggestion has not been advanced a second time, I presume it is quieted. As to the second, as to what the American Government think of our proposal at some time to operate a road in the United States, I will say another word beyond what I said a moment ago. 'The hon. member (Mr. Vien) thinks this is wholly unprecedented and that we should have asked the American Government what their attitude was going to be before we ventured1 to own any stock in the Grand Trunk Railway Company.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: To own all of the stock.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: To own all of the stock. I suppose they would be content for us to own a piece, but they would not stand for our owning any more, is that it? Where was it ever known before, he said, that one government operated a railroad in a country under the jurisdiction of another? I told him one instance precisely the same as this, not certainly where the mileage was so great, but exactly the same in kind. We operate now through the Canadian National Railway two lines in the United States. That does not satisfy the hon. member as an instance; he does not, T suppose, accept that as a precedent, so I will give him one or two more. He does not seem to be aware, although he poses as a critic here,-

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I am not posing at all.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Not posing?

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Well, the hon. gentleman put an interpretation to that word that I did not intend. He is really a critic. It is not a matter of pretence; it is a reality.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I am putting questions; I
am not criticising.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The hon. member says: Where is the precedent for the Government's operating railway lines in another country? I gave him one before; now I will give him a few more. Is he not aware that the American Government are operating not one but several lines in Canada to-day?
fHr. Vien.]

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The American Government?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Yes. They did not ask us for permission; they did not ask us what we thought of their action; they just went to work and operated them. They are operating the New York Central into the city of Ottawa.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: That is a temporary arrangement.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: They have running rights over the line.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The hon. member
draws a distinction again. I suppose he thinks that the American Government would let us operate a few lines a long time or many lines a short time.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Does the minister contend
that the American Government own the railways they are managing now? The American Government have temporarily taken over the management of a few lines with the intention, very often manifested, of handing them back to their private owners afterwards.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
has shifted his ground. A few moments ago it was not the ownership that was worrying him at all. He said: When you own the lines, how are you going to operate them; once you begin operating them, the trouble is going to come." It was the operating he was afraid of. When I show him that the American Government are now operating line after line, the New York Central into Ottawa, the Michigan Central in Ontario, the Great Northern in the West-

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Is it not true that these are merely running rights they have over the lines?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: No, the American Government are actually operating the railways as a Government, not through a company at all. The American Government did not say "by your leave" to this country.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The lines belong to Canadian railways, do they not and the American Government have running rights?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: To what Canadian railway does the New York Central belong?

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I understand they are
running over the Grand Trunk.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
No. What Canadian
railway does the Michigan Central belong to, or the Great Northern? Those are

American lines operating here just as the Grand Trunk operates in the United States.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Were those lines built in Canada by American companies?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Certainly, the Michigan Central was and the New York Central. What does it matter who built them, the American Government are operating them.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Is it not a fact that these lines are privately-owned lines, only taken over temporarily by the United States Government?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Very good. I am discussing operation now, because that is what the hon. member was on until he shifted off.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Then it is ownership that is the trouble? All right. We have owned lines in- the United States. Is it not just as harmful to own 100 miles of railway as 1,000?

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: It is ten times more harmful to own 1,000.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Would the hon. member say that we should ask the American Government's permission when we are getting 1,000 miles, and that when it was a case of a hundred miles it did not matter? What is the difference? If the hon. member had a point at all he should have stuck to operation. It is operation that the American Government and the American people [DOT]are concerned with. The American Government wants to see the road operated in the interests of their o-wn people. If there is any objection at all that you can conceive of, it would be with respect to operation and not to ownership. Ownership does not matter to them. There is precedent after precedent on their part, and at least one or two precedents on our part. Surely those are enough precedents to satisfy the hon. member. Does he think we should have gone to Washington and suggested to the American Government that it might take exception to bur going through with this transaction? I can conceive of nothing -I was going to say, more absurd. At all events, it would be most inexpedient and unwise. If the American Government has any representations to make it will make them.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: And you will have paid for the road.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
He says we shall have paid for the whole system and will only
have a part of it. Does he think the American Government may steal roads over there?

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: They might pay nothing for them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Will they not pay for them if they keep them?

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: They might pay nothing for them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: They are not going to steal any roads, so how shall we be paying for the whole road and getting only a part of it? The American Government, presumably, would be just as honest in dealing with a company whose stock was owned by the Dominion Government as in dealing with any other company. Would *the hon. member suggest that they would not? If negotiations subsequently take place with . the American Government we, as the shareholders of the *Grand Trunk, will be in the same position as the present shareholders are to-day. There is no difference in the world. Now, referring to the last question, how much money will it take? In the opinion of the authors of the Drayton-Acworth report it would take the amount the hon. gentleman stated.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: At that time. The Grand Trunk Railway asked to be heard before the Government in protest against the finding in that respect, and produced what they believed-and what appeared strong reasons for believing-that it would not take that amount, and that their road was in fair condition. They claim to be fully convinced that that is the case. In order to acertain which is right a thorough investigation will be necessary. We are satisfied that the margin between the two is not very great; there may be some difference. That investigation must precede the Board of Arbitration, and our evidence must go before that board just as it went in the case of the acquisition of the Canadian Northern stock. Our evidence will go before the Board of Arbitration in thorough form. The hon. member says that we cannot form a conclusion ourselves as to the condition the road is in.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: That has a bearing on the compensation to be paid, but it does not bear on the amount that the Government will find itself obliged to ask Parliament to vote.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
When we ask Parliament to vote a sum we will give full details.

We are not asking that now. It bears on the compensation to be paid.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: But we commit ourselves to come to that.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Certainly we do. I said that evidence would be produced to show what would be required. My hon. friend argued that we as members do not know anything about the condition of the road. He said that we could not tell simply by travelling over one line. " We all know," he said, " that the Toronto-Montreal road is good, and is one of the best equipped roads." If we all know that, cannot hon. members who travel over other lines know something about them? Surely we are as competent to judge of one line as another. We are not experts, but we know enough to know that there has been no substantial variation in upkeep [DOT]from the condition in 1916, and that is sufficient for our purpose. We will go before the Board of Arbitration and endeavour to establish our contention that owing to insufficient upkeep there should be a smaller amount paid for the stock. That is the place to bring forward those details.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: What amount has been expended on the Grand Trunk for maintenance per mile in 1916, 1917 and 1918, as compared with the Canadian Pacific expenditure?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If that information is not in this memoranda, it will certainly be given.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: What I mentioned, and what I think I said, was that $21,000,000 which should have been used for the maintenance of the road and rolling stock was diverted for dividend purposes. That appears on page 99 of the report.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
My own recollection is
the same as to the figures, and that is the amount we really ought to be discussing at this point. It may take more money for the road's requirements, but that extra money will all be represented in value in the road; that is to say, a terminal may be needed here and something else there, but that is not due to depreciation, but simply to the development of the concern. The figure which the hon. member (Mr. Vien) quoted is the figure that ought to be used when we are arguing on what sum the Drayton-Aoworth report finds should be spent in order to bring the road as it is now into a reasonable condition of upkeep. The Drayton-Acworth report says that that sum should have been used on the road in order to keep it up to a reasonable degree of maintenance, instead of being paid out in dividends. That is the amount in question in this connection.
My hon. friend (Mr. Fournier) will find the answer to his question on pages 48 and 49 of the memoranda. If he will look at the bottom of page 49 particularly, he will see that the maintenance of equipment figures are given as follows: 1918, $14,434,684, as against only $9,380,688 the year before, an increase of about 40 per cent; 1916, $7,329,455; 1915, $6,847,059.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Will the minister
complete the answer to my question by bringing down the railway statistics showing the Canadian Pacific Railway expenditures per mile?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The same expenditures -as the Grand Trunk Railway.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I can give those figures for I remember seeing them myself.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I must persist
in my previous question which the minister seems to treat lightly, that is, as regards the list of shareholders. The

minister says that it is very difficult to get that list because the list of to-day may be changed to-morrow. Surely it is easy to obtain the list of shareholders in the books of the company on the 9th of October. I hope the minister will get that list and table it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I doi not know how easy it will be. I have never made any inquiry regarding a single shareholder, and I do not think we are in the least con-'cerned as to that.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Public opinion
is under the impression,-to use a popular expression,-that there is a "nigger'' in the wood-pile, and we want to know who he is.
speakername: Mr. ARCH  A MB A TILT@

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
You will have toi hunt throught a hundred and eighty thousand sticks in the wood-pile to get at that nigger. Perhaps my hon. friend will mention the name of the individual. If he does we can the more easily find the nigger.
Mr. V1EN:	The minister knows his
name.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The minister is in a far better position than I am to mention the name.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
ilf my hon. frientd
depends on me for that information, then the name cannot be mentioned and we are done with that subject.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Can the minister tell us the direct obligation of the Grand Trunk Company to the Canadian people by reason of guarantees given by that company in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific? How much money would the Grand Trunk Company owe to the people to-day if we should insist upon their paying up all their obligations? Is it the intention of the Government that the money represented by those obligations shall be a credit in favour of Canada upon the award?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Any indebtedness owing by the Grand Trunk to the Government will certainly be a credit to the Government in the award. Any indebtedness of the Grand Trunk to the Government will have to be paid by the Grand Trunk before any of the shareholders can get anything.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Do you mean its loans?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Yes, certainly; all
indebtedness owing by the Grand Trunk. As to the Grand Trunk's obligations to the
Grand Trunk Pacific, that will be treated as an obligation on the part of the Grand Trunk Company and will be a liability the same as any other liability, to be considered by the arbitrators before any award at all is made in respect of this stock. The Grand Trunk Pacific obligations will be considered the same as all other obligations.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Will the minister give the exact figures as to how much the Government is claiming from the Grand Trunk to-day on account of these obligations?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The direct obligati ms
of the Grand Trunk to the Government are not very high.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Direct and indirect. They guaranteed .some bonds which we guaranteed afterwards and which we did not pay, and we fall back upon them for their guarantee. I should like to know how much is involved directly and indirectly.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
These figures will be
given exactly. I think they can be found in the book, but I will make a note of the question. I understand my honourable friend to ask for the amounts of money paid by the Government directly in respect of which the Grand Trunk was liable ahead of the Government. That is to say, supposing the Grand Trunk Company failed to pay the obligations in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific in regard to which it was liable ahead of any liability we might be under, and we paid the liability, the question is; what is the amount that the Grand Trunk owes us in the result? These figures can be given. But I want my honourable friend to understand this: the Grand Trunk made certain engagements in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific but did not meet them. They were not made by the Government direct. The loans were made by the Grand Trunk in aiding the Grand Trunk Pacific to pay the obligations itself. That is the way in which the main policy was pursued. So that no obligation direct from the Grand Trunk to the Government arises out of that. But the Grand Trunk's obligations in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific aggregated about five million dollars a year two years ago, and will aggregate about seven million dollars a year three years hence.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Do the officials of the Grand Trunk acknowledge that liability?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Certainly. They never disputed their liability on account of the Grand Trunk Pacific.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: They did not acknowledge it at the time the Drayton-Acworth report was made. They contended that the fact that the Government did not live up to the agreement of 1903 relieved them to a certain extent.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: They claimed that because of the Canadian Northern running through Northern Ontario, thus raising the cost of labour to them constituted a moral obligation. I do not think they seriously contend that they are relieved of their legal liability in regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The minister says that the Government will claim in the award the payment of all obligations of the Grand Trunk. I accept the assurance that the Government intend to make that claim, but will the minister make it clear in the resolution that that claim is to he regarded as a set-off?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I do not see how it could he anything else.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: That is the more reason why it should be made clear.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If it is clear already there is no reason why it should be made clearer.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: There is such a thing as making assurance doubly sure.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman can show that there is any doubt on the subject it will be made clear. Certainly any obligation of the Grand Trunk to the Government will be taken into account. If the arbitrators were to find that these stocks were worth fifteen million dollars but that the Grand Trunk owed the Government ten million dollars, then the stock would in reality be worth only five million.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The arbitrators would not he called upon to determine the claim of the Government but only the value of the stocks, unless there is a clear understanding that there is a set-off there will be trouble. It is not clear that the arbitrators are to sit in judgment upon the justice of the Government's claim.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Every claim that is made has to be established before the Board of Arbitrators, who musit be convinced that it is a good claim before they consider the determination of the value of the stock.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Does this contemplate that the arbitrators shall enter into the question of a set-off? They are only called

upon to fix the value of the stock. That is the beginning and end of their duties and I do not think they would have any right to enter into the other question. The Government would have to have recourse to some other means of establishing that claim as a set-off.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I do not agree with the hon. gentleman at all. The Government will claim every dollar that is owed them by the Grand Trunk.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: But that is not before the arbitrators.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Yes it is, everything is before the arbitrators that affects the value of the stock; the hon. gentleman will agree to that?

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Is not one thing that affects the value of the stock the debts of the company? Consequently, every debt of the company is before the arbitrators. A debt to the Government is just the same as any other debt and must 'be before the arbitrators. But let me say to my hon. friend, I will have the point he has raised looked into from the legal standpoint, and if there is any doubt it will be cleared uip.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Suppose the arbitrators value this stock at $15,000,000 and they find that the company is indebted to the Government to the extent of $20,000,000 there will be $5,000,000 coming back to the Government. But they could not value and arbitrate upon that if the arbitration is along the lines of the resolution. If the arbitration is along the lines of the resolution they can value the claim of the Government only by way of set-off to the valuation which they put upon the shares. If the claim of the Government is in excess of the value they put on the shares they must have some jurisdiction to give to the Government .a further judgment against the company.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The Government can
take steps to protect itself without their jurisdiction. In so far as the arbitration is concerned, the most favourable verdict the Government could get would be a declaration that the four stocks were worth nothing. Suppose the four stocks are in the view of the arbitrators worth nothing, the company will still owe us all the money they owed us before and the debt will be the same as it was before.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
It may be doubtful if you enter into an agreement that closes the whole of the negotiations that have been

taking place between the Government and the Grand Trunk.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows better than that, because he is a lawyer. We are arbitrating on the value of the shares. The Government is an entity on the one hand and the company is an entity on the other. The value is one thing and the debts owed to the Government are owed to the Government still. We may not be able to collect them, but we will be just as able to collect them as we are to-day. The company will not be worth one dollar less or one dollar more; it will be just in the same position exactly.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The minister does not wish to convey the suggestion to the committee that this arrangement that is proposed does not close the transaction between the Government and the company?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
It does not close them or open them up; it leaves them exactly as they are. We are arbitrating the value of the stock owned by the shareholders and not the value of anything owned by the company.
At six o'clock the Committee took recess.
After Recess.
The 'Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Does the Government intend to hold the Grand Trunk liable on the Grand Trunk Pacific agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The guarantees of the Grand Trunk Company with reference to the Grand Trunk Pacific have been mentioned two or three times to-day. Of course, the Grand Trunk will be held responsible for those guarantees in the arbitration proceedings. That is one of the things that the arbitrators must take into consideration.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: What annual expenditure would it involve on the part of the Grand Trunk to live up to those guarantees?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
In the papers that have been submitted there is a list of the bonds guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway, showing the total amount of interest liability. I quoted the list this afternoon. If the hon. gentleman will refer to page 51 he will read the following:
Guarantees by the Grand Trunk Railway Company have been made for the Grand Trunk Pacific of $97,301,253-$62,422,000 for principal and interest and $34,879,253 for interest only. Detail of this is in an attached statement. $25,000,000 of the foregoing total of
$6'2,422,000 is guaranteeing loans made by the Dominion Government.
That is the answer.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: How docs the Government arrive at the conclusion that the Grand Trunk is able to pay this liability of something like six or seven million dollars interest annually in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific, also to discharge the interest on the debenture stock and on the 4 per cent guaranteed stock, and still leave an equity to be arbitrated? Where does the minister get his figures from?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
will remember from the discussions that have taken place from time to time with reference to the loans made to the Grand Trunk Pacific that the Grand Trunk Railway Company has never paid out of earnings of the Grand Trunk Railway system any of the interest on the Grand Trunk Pacific guarantees. The interest on the guaranteed mortgages of the Grand Trunk Pacific have always been paid out of loans from time to time advanced by the Government. So that the old Grand Trunk system always had its full earnings to pay the interest on its debenture stock, its guaranteed stock, and its first, second, and third preference stock; and, <as has been shown, it always earned sufficient money to pay the interest, say $7,000,000 in round figures, on the original debenture stock issued for the construction of the old Grand Trunk railway and the purchase of the Great Western railway.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: What does the minister mean by always? The Grand Trunk Railway was incorporated in 1851.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: From 1851 onward the Grand Trunk Railway system always earned sufficient to pay interest on the debenture stock issued for the construction of the old Grand Trunk railway. Some years later-the date will be found in this sessional paper-the Grand Trunk Railway Company purchased the Great Western line and issued further debenture stock. From the time the company purchased that line it always earned sufficient to pay interest.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: On what?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
On the debenture stock issued for the purchase of the Great Western. Later the guaranteed stock was issued. Therefore, after having issued that guaranteed stock for other construction and improvements, 'the company was always able to earn a sufficient amount to pay the $7,000,000 interest on the stocks that I have

mentioned and t'he $2,500,000 interest on the guaranteed stock.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Since when?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Since the guaranteed stock was issued.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: When was that issued?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I could not give the date offhand, but it will be found: in the sessional paper. I will look it up and inform the hon. member a little later. But I say the Grand Trunk Railway Company was always able to pay that interest and still have- a surplus. The company then issued the first, second, and third preference stock, .the details of which are set out on page 56 of the sessional paper. The hon. member will see, starting from 1906, that the Grand Trunk Railway Company paid the interest on the guaranteed stock of 4 per cent; on the first preference stock of 5 per cent; on the second preference stock of 5 per cent; and on the third preference stock	of	3 per cent, or a total
of a little over $4,000,000. If the hon. member will refer to that statement, he will see that between 1906 and 1917 the Grand Trunk Railway Company paid the interest on its guaranteed stock annually, and also the interest on the first preference stock except in 1914 and 1910; and on the second preference stock it also paid the interest with the exception of those two years. On the third preference it paid the interest in 1906 and 1907, and also in 1910, 1911, 1012 and 1913. On the common stock, of course, it never paid any dividends at all. That stock was issued practically at the time the Grand Trunk Railway was built.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Let us get back to this 4 per cent guaranteed stock. The official reports of the London Stock Exchange show that the Grand Trunk did not pay 4 per cent on the guaranteed bonds all the time during the last ten years. Before that time it paid the interest in various amounts ranging from 2 to 3 per cent. What I want to know is how the Government arrives at the conclusion that this 4 per cent guaranteed stock has a value to-day, if we are to hold the Grand Trunk Railway Company liable for the Grand Trunk Pacific guarantee? In otheT words, how does the Government figure that there is any equity in this 4 per cent guaranteed stqck?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The honourable member I think stated that the Stock Exchange reports showed that the Grand Trunk Rail-
way Company had not paid any interest on the guaranteed stock for the last ten years.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Not all the time.
Mr. 3. D. REID:	Well, we have the
official document submitted to the House showing that the interest on the guaranteed stock was paid from 1906 down to 1916. There is not any doubt whatever about that.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: How about 1914?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
In 1914 the Grand
Trunk Railway Company paid 3i per cent instead of 4 per cent; in other words, they paid $2,129,166.67 dividends on the guaranteed stock instead of $2,433,333.33, or i per cent less. So that, during that ten year period they did pay the full interest with the exception of the i per cent in that particular year when the war started.
Now, the Grand Trunk Railway Company is liable in this way: it guaranteed the interest on a certain portion of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway bonds, and, as I understand it, the company agreed that it would not pay any dividends out of its earnings, until this bonded interest had been first paid. In other words, it defaulted in payment of that interest, it could not pay its shareholders any .dividends on their stock. That is where of course the company is in a very awkward position. If the company took the earnings that would ordinarily go to the shareholders in order to pay the interest on the guaranteed stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway,' then of course it would not have anything left for its own shareholders. That is why the company is pressing us to get a settlement so that it can be put in a position to pay dividends to its own shareholders.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Is it the intention then
of the Government to hold the Grand Trunk Company to its undertaking?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: So far as the debenture stock and this guaranteed stock is concerned, the Grand Trunk have always paid the dividends.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Not always.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Well, as I understand it, they have practically always paid them. During the last ten years anyway, with the exception of the last two war years, the old Grand Trunk has been paying the interest. Now, a large amount of money went into this railway for the first, second and third preference stock, as well as some $30,000,000 for the common stock. The Government agree to pay the dividend on the guaranteed stock, because it has been earned, and more besides. But if the arbitrators should decide not to allow the Grand Trunk any interest on the first,
second and third preferred stock and not to allow them anything for the common stock, the Company would certainly be paying a very heavy penalty for entering into the Grand Trunk Pacific arrangement.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Where do you arrive at the information that the Grand Trunk were able to pay this four per cent, or that they earned this four per cent? On what basis are you offering to pay, or did you offer to pay in the first place the $2,500,000, $3,000,000 and $3,600,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The basis is this: The interest has actually been paid for so many years; and the Drayton-Acworth report admitted that the company had earned and paid not only the $7,000,000, but also the average of $3,600,000 per annum-$2,500,000 of it on the guaranteed stock and $1,100,000 on the other. That statement in the Drayton-Acworth report is evidence for us, as is the statement of the Grand Trunk that they actually paid the dividends, not from capital but from actual earnings.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Then I understand the
minister to say that the Drayton-Acworth report is the basis upon which he is arguing; that is his starting point. He knows, of course, that the Drayton-Acworth report affirmed that those dividends should not have been paid; that they had been paid out of what should have gone to betterments and improvements; that the road did not earn dividends on the debenture stock and the cost of upkeep and maintenance of way. If that is the case, where does my hon. friend's argument land him?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The Drayton-Acworth report says that a portion of this amount that was paid out by way of dividend-not all-should have gone into the road. However, the Grand Trunk Railway Company take issue with that; they say that this statement in the report is not correct. But all of that will have to be brought before the board of arbitrators. If the company can convince the arbitrators that the report is wrong, the arbitrators will, of course, act accordingly. The Government will have their solicitor to take issue with them.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Where does the minister start from? What is the basis that he is working on? He does not accept the Drayton-Acworth report; he does not accept the Grand Trunk statement. On what information does he come to the conclusion that this $60,000,000 is valuable at all, and that after that is taken into consideration there might be something left to arbitrate? This seems to me to be a most absurd argument.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I do not think I can explain it more fully than I have; I have tried to explain the situation as well as I could. All I can say is that when the matter comes before the board of arbitrators the Government will take every possible step to put up their case and to secure whatever evidence they can to make the arbitration as lair as possible in the interest* of the Government.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: On the same basis as the Canadian Northern arbitration?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Personally I feel that
the solicitors who acted for the Government on the Canadian Northern arbitration were as good as there are in Canada.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Perhaps I shall be told that the answer has already been given, but it appears to me that the statement of affairs between tihe Government of Canada and the Grand Trunk Railway system has not yet been established, and that so far all the figures have not been given indicating what is actually due by the Grand Trunk Railway Company to the Dominion of Canada. In my opinion, the indebtedness of the Grand Trunk towards the Dominion of Canada is under three headings: First, the Grand Trunk has guaranteed the obligations of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and as the Grand Trunk Pacific is now the property of the Dominion of Canada

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: It is not yet.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Well, it is practically the same thing, and for the sake of argument, I take it for granted that it is, and the minister himself brought forward the argument that it is this .afternoon when he said that the .country would have control *of 22,000 miles of railway, for in that mileage he included the Grand Trunk Pacific.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: That is, after the arbitration.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: For the sake of argument, I am taking it for granted that sooner or later the Dominion of Canada will become sole proprietor of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. Starting from that point, I state first that the Grand Trunk Railway has guaranteed the obligations of the Grand Trunk Pacific to the amount of $97,301,253. I find this on page 51-and before going any further, I should like to ask the minister if I am correct in this.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I take it for granted that is correct, because those are the official statements that have been handed to me

and accordingly have been placed before the House.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Consequently, the first point is established, as to the liability of the Grand Trunk to the Grand Trunk Pacific and thence to the Dominion of Canada; that is, $97,301,253. Second, what is actually due directly by the Grand Trunk Railway to the Dominion of Canada? I do not know that an exact answer has been given this afternoon on this item. Third, what is due by the Grand Trunk Railway indirectly to the Dominion of Canada and on what account? It is only after these three items have been placed before the House that we shall be in a position to say exactly what is actually due by the Grand Trunk Railway to the Dominion of Canada. After these figures have been made available, I shall have something more to say about the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The hon. member asks for information as to what the Grand Trunk actually owe the Government, and also what they are liable for as far as the Dominion Government is concerned. I was just looking to see if I have that information here, but if not, I will furnish it. If I cannot look it up before we adjourn this evening, I will have it here to-morrow. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) tells me that the information is to be found on pages 51 and 52, where it says:
Besides the guarantees to the Grand Trunk Pacific, the 'Grand Trunk Railway Company have guaranteed the following:-
Then on page 52, we find:
Grand Trunk Railway Company, outstanding June 25, 1918:-
There is a list showing all their liabilities.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: On page 51 are given the liabilities of the Grand Trunk Railway Company in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific, but the liabilities of the Grand Trunk in respect of the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific guaranteed by the Government are not given. If I understand the maJtter aright, there are two classes of debentures of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. There is a class of debentures guaranteeed first by the Grand Trunk and second, by the Government, and there is a class of debentures guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway only.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Yes, hut the Grand Trunk Railway Company is not liable for the bonds guaranteed by the Government on the Grand Trunk Pacific.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Is not the Grand Trunk Railway Company guarantor to the Government of the bonds guaranteed by the Government for the Grand Trunk Pacific?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: No, it is not, it is liable only for what it guaranteed itself. The Grand Trunk Railway system is not liable for the bonds that were guaranteed by the Dominion Government.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Would it be possible to get from the minister an approximate figure as to the liabilities of the Grand Trunk to the Dominion of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The Grand Trunk Railway Company owes the Dominion of Canada some comparatively small amounts, and there are, I believe, counter accounts against that.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Do they run into tens of
millions?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
No. I look over the
Grand Trunk accounts and I do not find it so. I do not say that there is no obligation; I think there is; but it is not in large figures at all.- The Grand Trunk Railway Company did not borrow from the Government of Canada; it was the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company that borrowed, and the Grand Trunk in respect of those borrowings did not give its guarantee. I think it did in respect of one, and I am sure that will foe found in this pamphlet although it is difficult to trace it just at the moment. I find this on page 53:
$15,000,000-4 per cent Government loan, due July 1923, secured 'by Grand Trunk Pacific debentures and guaranteed Grand Trunk Railway.
That is one. On the same page I find:
$10,000,000'-4 per cent Dominion Government loan, due 'May, 1919, guaranteed by Grand Trunk Railway, secured by Grand Trunk Pacific bonds.
That is guaranteed by the Grand Trunk also, and that, I understand, was not paid.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: That is what I mean,

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: That is an outstanding liability by the Grand Trunk to the Government secured on the Grand Trunk Pacific.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Outside of the 597,000,000 owed by the Grand Trunk to the Dominion of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
No, it would not be right to say that the Grand Trunk owes this money to the Government. The Grand
Trunk Pacific owes it to the Government, and it is secured by bonds on the Grand Trunk Pacific. But the Grand Trunk is in the position of an obligor, as a guarantor of that debt, and consequently inability to collect from the Grand Trunk Pacific gives us right of recourse as against the Grand Trunk, and once we choose to exercise that right of recourse the Grand Trunk will then be compellable to pay, and this liability will, of course, necessarily be considered by the Board of Arbitration in deciding whether there is any value in the stock to be arbitrated upon. There are the liabilities of the Grand Trunk on 'bonds on the road that were initially guaranteed by the Grand Trunk. The first mortgage bonds are guaranteed by the Grand Trunk, the second mortgage bonds by the Government.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The first mortgage bonds by the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The first mortgage bonds by the Government, the second mortgage bonds by the Grand Trunk, and then those others come after that.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If the minister will look at page 26, there is an amount of $15,142,633 which is described as "exclusive of Government loan to Grand Trunk Railway." What does that mean?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I think that is the original loan made about the time of confederation or before.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Will that be paid back?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: That has never been considered. I think the people of Canada have pretty much come to the conclusion that that sum was a subsidy, although as far as I know it still stands in the position of a loan even legally at the present time. But, as I understand the matter, neither interest nor principal has even been requested from the Grand1 Trunk Company. That represents all that the Grand Trunk Company has secured in the way ol subsidies on its lines.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Has the Grand Trunk admitted its liability in respect of the guarantee of the Grand Trunk Pacific, or is it a matter of dispute as to whether they are legally liable to pay anything in respect of that guarantee?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I could not say that the Grand Trunk has admitted its liability. It has not done so in express documentary form, at all events. At the same time I could not say there is any question about



it. If I am asked my opinion I would say there is no question whatever about it. The Grand Trunk liability is absolutely intact.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: About what would that liability amount to?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: It all appears in these papers. That information will be found about page 50 and the next two or three pages.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: That is the $97,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
That is on page 51.
Guarantees by the Grand Trunk Railway Company have been made for the Grand Trunk Pacific of $97,201,253-$62,422,000 for principal and interest, and $34,879,253 for interest only. Detail of this is in an attached statement. Twenty-five million dollars of the foregoing total of $62,422,000 is guaranteeing loans made by the Dominion Government. That $26,000,000 covers the $10,000,000 and the $15,000,000 to which I have just referred. In so far as guarantees in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific are concerned, that would appear to be all.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Suppose the Government were to hold the Grand Trunk to their obligations in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific, about how much money would it take to settle their obligations?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: It would take the whole thing to settle it.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Yes, of course, because that is the liability. But the Grand Trunk will naturally claim: "We have security for that, we have the Grand Trunk Pacific." And, if they are able to show that that security is a commercial asset and affords ample protection, the arbitrators may find that that liability amounts to nothing. But in our opinion, in my opinion certainly, the arbitrators would not likely so find. If the security in the Grand Trunk Pacific was equal to the obligations against it, the'Grand Trunk would not have announced themselves two years ago at the end of their tether, nor have stated a few months ago that they could not operate the road any longer.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If the Grand Trunk were able to pay $30,000,000, would that relieve them of their obligations?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: It would not to me.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
What I want to get at is this. According to the stock exchange reports the total value of the first, second and

third preference and the common stock, on September II, 1919, was $28,000,000. That is all the assets that is left in the Grand Trunk to arbitrate. My hon. friend claims that $30,000,000 would not offset their obligations. Then why do you guarantee the $27,000,000 worth of what is called guaranteed stock? Why do you guarantee that stock and put it out of your reach if you are going to hold the Grand Trunk to their obligations?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Does not my hon. friend see that the $28,000,000-I do not know whether he has figured it rightly-is the value as reflected in the market, and in that reflection the Grand Trunk's liability was taken into account. Does he imagine that anybody who buys Grand Trunk stock pays no attention to Grand Trunk liabilities, including its liabilities to the Grand Trunk Pacific? So if the reflection in the market is a correct reflection-and personally I do not think so-the Government would have to assume the liabilities, including the Grand Trunk Pacific, and pay this besides.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Certainly not.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The hon, member
shakes his head and smiles as if I did not understand it.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: We will hear my hon. friend at it.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The minister said this
afternoon he did not understand much about stocks. I can believe that. The total value of these stocks as reflected by the stock exchange is $28,000,000. The minister just stated that he would not consider $30,000,000 a sufficient sum to settle the Grand Trunk's liability to Canada. But there is another asset in the Grand Trunk at the present time, and until this legislation goes through, amounting to $27,000,000 more, and that is the $60,000,000 worth of guaranteed stock quoted in the market at 45. That makes its value $27,000,000. In the last few days it has gone up to 60, which means that my hon. friend has made it possible for some persons to gain $9,000,000 on account of this legislation. My hon. friend takes precautions to make this $60,000,000 worth of stock safe from the actions of the Canadian Government in respect of the Grand Trunk's liability to the Grand Trunk Pacific, and he only leaves himself about $28,000,000, if that is the worth of the stock, to cover the total obligations of the Grand Trunk with respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific. I do not see

how my hon. friend can get away from the fact that he is giving away the assets of the people of Canada when he guarantees pay-,ment on a stock that has paid 4 per cent at times, less at other times, and has- failed to pay a dividend in the last two years, on the ground that the people who own that stock own something. As a means of getting even with them we are going to guarantee this stock. I cannot understand my hon. friend's process of reasoning.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I thoroughly agree that the hon. gentleman does not understand it. It is difficult to tell where to start to disentangle the lot of absurdities that the hon. gentleman puts before the committee.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: You said that last year.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
He says that $28,000,-
000 is the market value of the three preference stock and the common stock, and $27,000,000 the market value of the guaranteed .stock. Now we- are arbitrating on what we should pay for these three preference and the common stocks. He says that they are only worth in the market $28,000,000, and the company's liability is $30,000,000 in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific. I told him a moment ago, and I am sure if he will give his mind a chance he will see it, that those who are estimating the market value of Grand Trunk stock estimate it less because of its Grand Trunk Pacific liabilities. Is not that so? Does my hon. friend mean to suggest that if the Grand Trunk had not its Grand Trunk Pacific entanglements its stock would not be worth more in the market-I will go step by step slowly and give the hon. gentleman every chance-Is not that correct? Of course, it would be worth more. That is to say, it is worth less to-day because of those liabilities. So far as the estimate of the market buyers is concerned, we can afford to pay $27,000,000 for the three preference stocks and the common stock, assume the Grand Trunk liabilities and come out exactly even. Is not that correct? So we have $27,000,000 to come and go upon if their estimate is correct. I would refuse to accept their estimate. I think it is high. But we leave it to the arbitrators; that is all there is to it.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: But before you leave it to them, you take away this $60,000,000 of stock which they might have to pay over to the Dominion Government.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Oh, no.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
They have ninety-seven million dollars of a liability and in order to make them safe you guarantee this stock
66*
and convert it into practically Dominion Government bonds and then you only leave them this twenty-eight million dollars of more or less worthless stock to arbitrate upon. You do not mean to say that you are going to take a mortgaged property to meet all this liability. Of course, not. You know better than that. So you virtually make this sixty million dollars a mortgage, *or bond, or debenture-whatever you wish to call it-and place this in their hands, and it only leaves $28,000,000 worth of stock to deal with. So that if their obligation is $30,000,000 you know you are $2,000,000 short to start with, but you' will arbitrate to see if there is a value still in the $28,000,000 worth of stock. You say that $30,000,000 would be less than you would expect to settle the whole undertaking. There is absolutely no reason in the argument, and I venture to say that when my hon. friend is through with the transaction he will find that he has let the Dominion of Canada in for a vast sum of money, releasing the Grand Trunk Pacific from their obligation as far as this $60,000,000 is concerned. All the Dominion may take is $28,000,000 of more or less worthless stock for an obligation of $97,000,000.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If I understood the Minister of Railways correctly this afternoon, he said that in taking over the'Grand Trunk we were assuming the bonded debt of the Grand Trunk Pacific.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: 'Well, no. There is no specific assumption of that liability.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Is there not $70,000,000 worth of Grand Trunk Pacific bonds which are guaranteed by the old Grand Trunk?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: There is a large amount.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Do we not become responsible for the payment of those bonds?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: No more than we are to-day.	[DOT]

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The minister said that for ten years the Grand Trunk had been able to distribute a million dollars a year in dividends. Was not this because the Government paid interest on Grand Trunk Pacific bonds which were guaranteed by the old Grand Trunk?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If the Grand Trunk had paid interest due on Grand Trunk Pacific bonds would it have been able to pay dividends to its shareholders?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: It would not have been able to within the last two or three years. The Grand Trunk Pacific paid its own dividends, but it paid them because we lent them .money, on the security of the Grand Trunk Pacific, to do so. Now, the Grand Trunk has its own liabilities in relation to the Grand Trunk Pacific. If, in the minds of the arbitrators, those liabilities are greater than the Grand Trunk Pacific is .security for, the award will be reduced accordingly. But we will certainly argue- and I think correctly-that if the Grand Trunk Company is called on to discharge its liabilities to the Grand Trunk Pacific, the fact being that the Grand Trunk Pacific cannot discharge them itself, then they would be in a position to pay dividends on these four stocks.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If the Grand Trunk Pacific went into liquidation or failed to earn its fixed charges, would not the old Grand Trunk have to pay about $3,000,000 a year interest on the Grand Trunk Pacific bonds which are not guaranteed?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Yes, or more than that.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If it paid interest on these bonds would there be any possibility of its paying dividends upon any of its preferred stock?	,

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: There would be a possibility, of course.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If it did not pay, then what would be the value of the preferred stock?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I would not be a very good judge of that. One reason that would make it difficult to judge of that would be that the common stock lies there for which $30,000,000 was paid but on which no dividend has ever been paid, and the prospect has never been darker than the last year. But it has always had a value. It would be impossible for me to say that the preferred stock would have no value.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: My hon. friend must have all the information. Would he read to the Committee the letter written by Sir Alfred Smithers to Sir Robert Borden three years ago in which the statement was made that the Grand Trunk was at the end of its tether?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I have read the letter.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Will the Government say that it is possible for the Grand Trunk to earn enough to pay a dividend upon its debentures and guaranteed stock and also 
to pay the interest upon the Grand Trunk Pacific bonds which it has guaranteed?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: We certainly would not say it could. We will argue that it could not. The Grand Trunk, on the other hand, say: "We ought to be permitted to make a revenue, and we certainly cannot make it unless we are given rates which are reasonable under conditions such as now obtain." In a word, everything depends on rates. It would be possible for them to do it if the rates were higher, but the Government will argue that to keep the rates at a reasonable figure, having regard to all conditions, they could not discharge their obligations to the Grand Trunk Pacific and pay dividends on the preferred stock or any stock. That is our contention.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Will the minister say, in view of its commitments in respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific, that the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada is a solvent concern?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Well, we will argue that they could not pay dividends and discharge all their obligations. But I am sure the Grand Trunk will argue very strenuously that they could. I am not in the position of a judge in the matter; that will be for the arbitrators to decide.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If it is not a solvent concern how can either its preferred stock or any stock have any value, and what is there to arbitrate?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If the judges find that it is not solvent they will find that the value is nothing; that is all. My fion. friend must see that the long series of questions he has asked rests on the answer to one, and when that answer is given there is not very much object in answering the rest.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The minister will
pardon me if I put another question. Could not the Government obtain the Grand Trunk by liquidation without paying anything for dither preferred or common stock?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
That is something
which, to answer with certainty, would require the gift of prophecy as well as of business judgment. It would depend upon many circumstances. It would depend upon the action of the Railway Commission with regard to rates, and also upon the attitude and intentions of other railway people as to the Grand Trunk. It might well be that there are railroad people in the

world-perhaps in Canada-who could save the Grand Trunk from the position by enlarging their own system.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: So is the debenture stock.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: duce something from nothing. What you are adding in the present instance is the guarantee of the Dominion of Canada, which is worth money. You are making a present to the Grand Trunk Railway Company outside of the fact that you are buying the concern. It is all right to buy the concern if you want to, but you should not buy the concern and make a present to the holders of the debenture stock and the four per cent guaranteed stock.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: My hon. friend has overlooked one important fact in the argument he has made, and it is this: The guaranteed stock is in a real sense a preference stock.
