subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Is it the intention that the Grand Trunk, for instance, to mention only that company, will remain in perpetuity under its present name and not lose its identity under the ownership of the Government ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I cannot say that any fixed determination of policy has been come to, but I would say that itf was entirely probable, after the acquirement is completed, that the road would be merged in the ,

Canadian National system and thereby lose its name.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
What would become of this stock on which we are guaranteeing the interest if the company disappears altogether? Suppose, for instance, the company is wound up and goes out of existence?
Mr. ME1GHEN: The company does not need to become extinct to have the system merged. For instance, the Canadian Northern system owned, I think, twenty-nine separate companies, all of which were distinct entities and had stock issues. They were creations of the Canadian Northern, and became a part of the system. The stock issues still remain. The Grand Trunk stock may still be outstanding; that is to say, the non-voting certificates, as it is better to call them, may still be outstanding, although the system as a system is merged in the Canadian National railway system, and run as part of that system. That answers the question fully. These non-voting certificates, or as you may call it, this non-voting stock, will be held by the owners of the present stock, and they will cash their dividends just as Victory Loan certificates are cashed, while the Grand Trunk will be merged with the Canadian National railway and be known as such.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I can see no utility or purpose in having so many different companies and so many names when we own the property. The Intercolonial, for instance, which is a Government property nearly fifty years old, has no incorporation of any kind. It has no stock and never had any stock. It is owned by the Government, but it is no more owned by the Government than is the Canadian Northern. The Canadian Northern is also owned by the Government except for a few outstanding shares here and there. I think the man in the street would prefer that we shoulu own the Canadian Northern as we own the Intercolonial, and that if we are going to own the Grand Trunk we should own it in the same way as we do the Intercolonial. If we are going to own the Grand Trunk let us own it in unison with the other properties we have. There is no use in having a number of different names and a variety of stocks and bonds and debentures. If we are going to own the whole road the simpler way would be for the Government to own all these properties and deal with them, so far as book-keping and management is concerned, just as we deal with the Intercolonial.
However, that is a matter of detail. The member for Royal (Mr. H. H. McLean) asked the Minister of Railways something about the policy of the Government in regard to the port of Portland and the ports of St. John and Halifax. The minister will remember that when the scheme of building the Transcontinental railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific was being considered, a part of the bargain, so far as the people were concerned, was that any freight that was not routed by the owner was to be routed by the Government. The present Government was not in power then, but the principles of governments do not die and obligations of one government must [DOT] ndbessarily be carried on by the other; it is the King's business, which must be carried on. I would remind the Minister of Railways that it is an outstanding policy of the Government of this country that all freights originating in Canada which are not Touted by the owner must go by Canadian ports. It i.s desirable to know if the Government is going to stand by that principle. Of course, there was no written agreement between the Canadian people and the Government, but that was announced as the policy of the Canadian Government, and I never heard that this Government had in any way departed from [DOT]the policy established by their predecessors. Now that there is talk of acquiring an American outlet for Canadian products, it would be interesting to know if it is the [DOT]intention to depart from that policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I do not know that I oan give any more complete answer than I gave to the hon. member for Royal. When we build our Canadian poTts we certainly intend to use them. We have made a short connection to St. John by taking over, I think, the St.. John Valley line; and we all know that thei shortest ]rail and oc/ean route between Liverpool and Canada is via Halifax. The Government will use its own ports and give them preference.

speechtext: Is the minister prepared to tell the people that all the traffic collected on the new Grand Trunk line from Western United States and Western Canada, having reached Montreal, will be forwarded direct to St. John and Halifax instead of being diverted from Montreal to Portland? The people of Canada, and more particularly the people of the Maritime Provinces, are interested to know what will he done in the future.

subsubtopic: RESOLUTION RESPECTING ITS ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.

I do not know that 1 can add anything to what I have said. We

will use our own road to St. John and Halifax. The Government are not changing the policy laid down since we came into power in 1911. We are developing the ports of Halifax and St. John and we shall certainly use them.
